# Panorama: Fast-Track Nearest Neighbors

### ABSTRACT

Candidate _verification_ is the primary bottleneck in Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search (ANNS) pipelines for high-dimensional neural embeddings. We introduce Panorama, a state-of-the-art refinement technique that accelerates verification by exploiting the inherent spectral decay of these embeddings. Using PCA to compact signal energy, Panorama evaluates candidate distances incrementally. At each step, it computes a strict lower bound on the full-vector distance, dynamically pruning candidates the moment this bound exceeds the running _k_-th nearest neighbor distance. While PCA’s concentration of variance facilitates pruning, it breaks the uniform-variance assumption required by Product Quantization (PQ). To resolve this, we introduce a variance-shaping step that redistributes energy across subvectors to render accretive refinement compatible with quantized indexes. Optimized for modern memory hierarchies via vectorized bulk-pruning and cache-conscious data layouts, Panorama has been upstreamed into the Faiss library across major index families (IVFPQ/Flat, HNSW, and Refine). Panorama achieves higher QPS at any target recall with a cost that provably scales inversely with dataset spectral decay, delivering end-to-end speedups of up to 28.9\(\times\) and outperforming probabilistic methods across all recall bands.

### 1 INTRODUCTION

The proliferation of large-scale neural embeddings has transformed machine learning applications, from computer vision and recommendation systems [27, 32] to bioinformatics [1] and retrieval- augmented generation (RAG) pipelines [18, 29]. As embedding models produce vectors with thousands of dimensions--OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-large [41] reaches 3072--the need for real-time Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search (ANNS) intensifies.

_The refinement bottleneck._ Current ANNS methods fall into four major families: _graph-based_ (HNSW [37], DiskANN [43]), _clustering- and-quantization-based_ (IVFPQ [24, 25], ScaNN [20]), _tree-based_ (kd-trees [7], FLANN [40]), and _hash-based_ (LSH [3, 23], multi- probe LSH [35]). All families share a pipeline of two phases [5]: _filtering_ reduces the database to a set of candidates \(\Gamma\) and _refinement_ (verification) selects _k_ candidates nearest to the query. Prior work in ANNS has almost exclusively targeted the filtering phase, assuming that refinement is inconsequential. This assumption holds on low- dimensional embeddings; on modern neural embeddings, however,

refinement consumes most of end-to-end query latency, with the share rising monotonically in dimensionality [16].

_Why existing remedies underperform._ Prior work addresses the refinement bottleneck primarily through _probabilistic_ distance estimation: ADSampling [16] randomly subsamples coordinates, while FINGER and KS2 [11, 34] approximate inner products via angle estimation. Consequently, these methods hit a structural recall ceiling and cannot guarantee exact k-NN regardless of the time budget. Furthermore, they are poorly suited for cluster-based indexes that utilize sequential scans. PDX [28] mitigates the memory bottleneck via a columnar layout, yet suffers this same recall deficiency or, in its deterministic variant PDX-BOND, low throughput. Finally, none of these approaches composes with _product quantization_ (PQ) [25], a ubiquitous compression primitive in billion-scale ANNS. This paper introduces Panorama, a deterministic and hardware-friendly refinement method that eliminates this compromise. By providing a mathematically principled pruning bound, Panorama delivers superior throughput at _every_ target recall band--up to and including 100% recall--while natively integrating with PQ and other existing index families.

_Contributions._ Our contributions are as follows:

\(\bullet\) **Accretive refinement.** Panorama accumulates _L_<sub>2</sub> distance terms incrementally along the PCA basis, maintains tight Cauchy- Schwarz lower bounds on the fly, and prunes any candidate whose lower bound exceeds the running _k_th-nearest-neighbor threshold. This pruning is controlled by a tunable parameter \(\varepsilon\), exact at \(\varepsilon=1\), and relaxed for the sake of efficiency with \(\varepsilon<1\). This scheme fits into graph, tree, clustering, and hash-based indexes without changing their filtering phase.

\(\bullet\) **Theoretical grounding.** We show that the expected verification cost scales inversely with an exponential PCA decay factor observed in real-world embeddings (Proposition 5.1) and generalize this guarantee to out-of-distribution queries (Proposition 5.2).

\(\bullet\) **Compatibility with product quantization.** While PCA’s aggressive variance concentration aids pruning, it destabilizes downstream product quantization (PQ) and erodes recall. To counteract this, we apply an orthogonal transformation _R_ that flattens coordinate variances to a target diagonal \(t\prec\lambda\) while preserving covariance eigenvalues \(\lambda\). We construct _R_ by a Robin Hood sequence of Haar-random rotations that transfers surplus variance across PQ blocks, followed by an intra-block Haar-random rotation to reduce residual anisotropy. Together, these steps preserve PCA’s pruning efficacy while ensuring PQ compatibility.

Panorama is available in Faiss across HNSW, IVFPQ, IVFFlat, and a PQ-refine step (FastScan-Refine), delivering up to 28.9\(\times\) end-to-end speedups.

## 2 RELATED WORK

Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search (ANNS) pipelines generally operate in two phases: a filtering phase that retrieves a candidate set, and a refinement phase that computes exact distances to find the true top-_k_ neighbors. Historically, the literature has heavily optimized the filtering phase. _Graph-based methods_ \[36, 37, 43\], _tree- based partitions_ \[7, 40\], and _Locality-Sensitive Hashing_ (LSH) \[23, 35\] all employ distinct spatial navigation strategies to reduce the candidate pool. However, as embedding dimensionalities grow, the exact distance evaluations required at the leaves, neighborhoods, or hash buckets of these structures become the dominant computational bottleneck. Panorama is designed to operate atop any of these filtering structures to accelerate this final distance computation.

_Clustering-and-quantization methods_ partition space and compress vectors to reduce storage and accelerate search. IVF \[24\] builds inverted indexes via _k_-means clustering to map queries to nearby centroids. IVFPQ \[25\] applies _product quantization_ (PQ) within clusters, decomposing vectors into independently quantized subvectors. Advanced variants further minimize quantization error via learned rotations (OPQ \[19\]), multi-cluster assignments (Multi-D-ADC \[6\]), anisotropic quantization (SeaNN \[20\]), or by introducing theoretical error bounds for extreme quantization (RaBitQ \[17\]).

While these methods excel at compression, scanning encoded vectors remains a computational bottleneck, as traditional implementations require exhaustive distance calculations across all subvectors. Recent approaches address this limitation by optimizing both storage and scanning. Variance-Aware Quantization (VAQ) \[42\], for instance, abandons PQ’s uniform bit-budget to adapt dictionary sizes proportionally to each subspace’s explained variance. Crucially, VAQ bypasses exhaustive scanning by employing triangle inequality bounds and early-abandoning heuristics to mathematically prune candidates on the fly. While VAQ addresses variance skew by heavily modifying the underlying quantizer, Panorama does the exact opposite: we introduce an orthogonal spectrum-shaping transformation that flattens the data’s variance. This ensures strict compatibility with highly-optimized, uniform PQ implementations while preserving enough front-loaded energy to power accretive early-abandoning.

Beyond quantization, dedicated _refinement techniques_ attempt to accelerate the final distance computations directly. Probabilistic methods such as ADSampling \[16\], PDX \[28\], and FINGER \[11\] rely on stochastic sub-sampling or proxy metrics, which intrinsically degrade maximum recall. Conversely, exact refinement methods, including BOND \[13\] and Stepwise \[26\], establish strict distance bounds to prevent false dismissals but suffer from loose bounds. By forgoing probabilistic estimation in favor of mathematically rigorous Cauchy-Schwarz bounds along a shaped PCA basis, Panorama<tbc>

<tbc>generates tight pruning bounds, allowing it to exceed the throughput of probabilistic methods across all recall bands.

Finally, some works refer to refinement over \(k'=k_\text{factor}\cdot k\) over-fetched candidates as ‘_reranking_’ (e.g., using coarse indices like IVFPQFastScan \[4\] for rapid initial retrieval followed by unquantized _k_NN). Because Panorama accelerates the underlying mathematical operations of distance computation, it serves as a drop-in replacement to accelerate this exact reranking stage as well.

## 3 PANORAMA: DISTANCE COMPUTATION

Problem 1 (_k_NN refinement). _Given a query vector_ \(\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) _and a candidate set_ \(\Gamma=\{\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_N\}\)_, find the set_ \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq\Gamma\) _such that_ |S|=_k and_ \(\forall\mathbf{s}\in\mathcal{S},\mathbf{x}\in\Gamma\backslash\mathcal{S}:\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{s}\|_2\le\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|_2\).

Problem 2 (ANN index). _An_ approximate nearest neighbor _index is a function_ \(\mathcal{I}:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{D}\rightarrow 2^{|\mathbb{D}|}\) _that maps a query_ **q** _and a database_ D _to a candidate set_ \(\Gamma=\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{q},\mathbb{D})\)_, where_ \(\Gamma\) _contains the true k-nearest neighbors with high probability._<sup>1</sup>

Problem 1 is the computational bottleneck: with _N_ candidates, naive refinement computes \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}_i\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^d(\mathbf{q}_j-\mathbf{x}_{i,j})^2\) for each candidate, requiring \(\Theta(N\cdot d)\) operations.

_Accretive bounds._ We decompose the squared Euclidean distance through a norm-preserving orthogonal transform \(T:\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^d\), following Kashyap and Karras \[26\]:<tbc>

\(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2=\|T(\mathbf{q})\|^2+\|T(\mathbf{x})\|^2-2\langle T(\mathbf{q}),T(\mathbf{x})\rangle.\) (1)

<tbc>Given thresholds \(0=m_0<m_1<\cdots<m_L=d\) that partition the dimensions into _L_ levels, we define partial inner products and tail (residual) energies:

\(p^{(\ell_1,\ell_2)}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})=\sum_{j=m_{\ell_1}+1}^{m_{\ell_2}}T(\mathbf{q})_jT(\mathbf{x})_j,R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(\ell_1,\ell_2)}=\sum_{j=m_{\ell_1}+1}^{m_{\ell_2}}T(\mathbf{q})_j^2,R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(\ell_1,\ell_2)}=\sum_{j=m_{\ell_1}+1}^{m_{\ell_2}}T(\mathbf{x})_j^2.\) (2)

The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality \[21\] yields a monotonically tightening lower bound on the squared distance:

\(\text{LB}^\ell(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})=R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(0,d)}+R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(0,d)}-2\big(p^{(0,\ell)}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})+\sqrt{R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(\ell,d)}R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(\ell,d)}}\big)\le\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2.\) (3)

We further introduce a _pruning aggressiveness_ parameter \(\epsilon\in[0,1]\). At level \(\ell\), the distance comprises an exact accumulated term minus the unknown tail inner product. Let \(A^\ell=R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(0,d)}+R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(0,d)}-2p^{(0,\ell)}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\) and \(C^\ell=\sqrt{R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(\ell,d)}R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(\ell,d)}}\). The strict Cauchy-Schwarz bound subtracts the worst-case tail term \(2C^\ell\); reducing this correction gives the relaxed score:

\(\text{LB}_\epsilon^\ell(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})=A^\ell-2\epsilon C^\ell.\) (4)

<sup>1</sup>Some indexes like HNSW interleave filtering and refinement; we treat the exact- distance computations on visited nodes as the refinement phase.

<tbc>_Soundness at_ \(\varepsilon=1\). Setting \(\varepsilon=1\) recovers the exact Cauchy- Schwarz lower bound (Equation (3)), so pruning cannot remove any candidate that could still enter the top-_k_ over the candidate set. Lowering \(\varepsilon\) relaxes this worst-case tail correction to enable more aggressive pruning and higher throughput, trading off strict exactness for a controlled recall-throughput knob. As Figures 6 and 7 show, this relaxation consistently yields superior performance at any recall target while the strict mode remains available whenever exact refinement is needed.

_Algorithm._ Algorithm 1 is the Panorama refinement loop. It maintains a heap _H_ of exact _k_NN distances seen so far, initialized on the first _k_ candidates, and the associated _k_<sup>th</sup> smallest distance d<sub>k</sub>. For each subsequent batch, it advances all candidates one level at a time, prunes any with lower bound \(\mathrm{LB}_\varepsilon^\ell(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})>d_k\) (Line 8), and bulk-commits the survivors’ exact distances to _H_ at the final level (Lines 12-14). As memory layouts across state-of-the-art indexes vary wildly, we decouple the pruning strategy from the layout via the _batch size_ parameter _B_:

When the index organizes contiguously (IVFFlat, IVFPQ), we set _B_ to 1024 to balance systems affordances with pruning power, as discussed in Section 6.1. When candidates arise non- contiguously (HNSW, Refine), we set _B_=1: the inner batch loop collapses and each candidate is early-abandoned at its first offending level, which is the only feasible mode under scattered memory access. Section 6 elaborates on the systems consequences.

Let \(\rho_i\in\{m_0,\dots,m_L\}\) be the dimension at which candidate **x**_<sub>i</sub>_ is pruned (or survives, with \(\rho_i=d\)). The total cost is \(\sum_{i=1}^N\rho_i\), so with \(\phi=\frac{\mathbb{E}[\rho]}{d}\) the average fraction of dimensions processed, the expected cost is \(\mathcal{O}(\phi dN)\). We make this scaling precise in Section 5.

Panorama relies on (i) a transform _T_ that concentrates energy in leading dimensions, enabling tight bounds--achieved through PCA (Section 4) and (ii) level thresholds \(m_\ell\) that balance the per-level control overhead against pruning granularity.

## 4 TRANSFORM AND VARIANCE SHAPING

The scheme of Section 3 reduces the distance estimation per can didate **x** and level \(\ell\) to the geometric mean \(\sqrt{R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(\ell,d)}}R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(\ell,d)}\) of tail energies. This quantity drops for each **x** as \(\ell\) grows; when it falls below the running gap between **x**’s known distance and the current _k_<sup>th</sup> distance, **x** is ruled out of the _k_NN set, hence we stop reading its coordinates. The task of the orthogonal transform _T_ is to make those trailing tail energies shrink promptly.

This section addresses the following two questions:

\(\bullet\) _Which_ orthogonal transform shrinks the tail most effectively (§4.1)? We argue that PCA is the natural answer: a closed-form, data-adaptive transform that minimizes the expected tail energy at each level, and whose spectrum yields the decay rate.<tbc>

\(\bullet\) _How_ do we reconcile PCA with product quantization (PQ), given that PCA breaks PQ’s uniform bit-budget assumption (§4.2)? We amend PCA with a process that evens out energy between and within PQ blocks while retaining most of its front-loading.

### 4.1 PCA as the closed-form transform

Given a dataset \(\mathcal{D}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) with empirical covariance \(\Sigma\), PCA (_principal component analysis_) returns the orthogonal matrix \(T\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) whose rows are the eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\), ordered so that the corresponding eigenvalues satisfy \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge 0\). As an orthogonal transform, PCA preserves Euclidean geometry: \(\|T(\mathbf{x})\|_2=\|\mathbf{x}\|_2\) and \(\|T(\mathbf{q})-T(\mathbf{x})\|_2=\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|_2\), hence transformed vectors retain the distance decomposition of Equation (1) and the lower bound of Equation (3) is _lossless_. PCA is singled out among orthogonal transforms by its energy _distribution_ across coordinates.

_Why PCA is the right basis?_ Orthogonal transforms conserve energy: the total \(\sum_j\|T(\mathbf{x})_j\|^2=\|\mathbf{x}\|^2\) is fixed, so any reduction in tail energy arises by moving energy into leading coordinates. The movable amount is determined by the spectrum of \(\Sigma\) via a classical variational fact (Ky Fan / Schur-Horn \[21\]): the maximum energy that an orthogonal transform can place in the first _m_ coordinates is \(\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j\), attained when the leading rows of _T_ span the top-_m_ eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\)--which is exactly what PCA provides. PCA is therefore optimal at every level simultaneously, leaving the smallest possible expected tail \(\sum_{j>m}\lambda_j\).

_How about other orthogonal transforms?_ Two alternatives--the Discrete Cosine Transform \[44\] and the Haar wavelet basis \[38\]-- also concentrate energy into leading coordinates, but only provided that the data has strong _local self-similarity_, i.e., adjacent coordinates of correlated values, as in smooth signals or natural images. These _fixed_ (non-data-adaptive) bases succeed when the data already aligns with them. In unstructured embedding spaces such as text representations and learned features, no such locality exists, hence these fixed bases do not improve on the original axes. By contrast, PCA’s eigenvectors are by definition the directions of maximum variance _in the data at hand_, hence PCA adapts to the data’s covariance structure. As Figure 1 illustrates, PCA compacts energy more than DCT and Haar wavelet transforms, regardless of the underlying data.

<tbc>We define the expected residual energy at level _m_ as the normalized PCA tail variance,<tbc>

\(E(m)=\frac{\sum_{j=m+1}^d\lambda_j}{\sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j},\)

<tbc>i.e., the fraction of total variance retained by the trailing _d-m_ coordinates. Across all six datasets in our study, _E(m_) is modeled well by the exponential:

\(E(m)\approx e^{-\alpha\frac{m}{d}},\)

with a data-specific constant \(\alpha>0\) obtained from the empirical PCA spectrum. Figure 2 reports the empirical _E(m_) and the fitted exponential on each dataset; confirming that the exponential model is faithful to the data. This shape is what classical spectral theory predicts for analytic covariance kernels--smooth neural embeddings (GELU, softmax) and Gaussian-family kernels among them; we develop the connection in Section 5. Here, \(\alpha\) is a measured number per dataset. Larger \(\alpha\) denotes that the tail collapses more rapidly, hence the Cauchy-Schwarz remainder shrinks, and Panorama prunes earlier. We concretize the connection in Section 5, showing that the expected refinement cost scales as \(\frac{Nd}{\alpha}\) .

## 4.2 Spectrum shaping for PQ-compatibility

PCA is excellent for pruning alone, as it aggressively concentrates variance into the leading dimensions. However, in the IVFPQ index, Panorama has to coexist with product quantization (PQ), which clashes with that concentration. We recall how PQ works, explain why PCA breaks it, and describe the two-stage procedure that fixes the problem while preserving most of PCA’s compaction.

_What PQ expects._ Product quantization [25] splits each _d_-dimensional vector into _M_ contiguous subvectors of size _d/m_ and quantizes each subvector with its own 2_<sup>n</sup>_bits-entry codebook learned by _k_- means. Each subvector receives the same number of code bits, under<tbc>

<tbc>the implicit assumption that variance is even across subvectors. If one subvector carries almost all the energy, an equal-bit codebook leads to underrepresentation of the data; if another subvector is almost constant, the codebook budget is wasted on noise.

_Why raw PCA breaks PQ._ The concentration of energy in the first dimensions, which confers to PCA a pruning advantage, clashes with PQ. As the leading subvectors carry nearly all the variance and the trailing ones collapse to near-constant, PQ underserves the informative leading blocks while wasting a fixed-bit budget on near-zero blocks. To use Panorama with IVFPQ, we should reconcile the PCA per-level energies with PQ, while retaining most of the front-loading that facilitates pruning. We do so in two steps: a coarse _inter-level_ redistribution of energy among levels (i.e., blocks), followed by a fine _intra-level_ isotropization that spreads each level’s energy over its dimensions.

_Procedure 1: Robin Hood inter-level shaping._ We split the _d_ PCA coordinates into _L_ contiguous levels of size _b=d/L_, which we use to refine bounds. Let \(E_\ell=\sum_{j=(\ell-1)b+1}^{\ell b}\lambda_j\) be the energy of level \(\ell\). PCA endows the leading levels more than the trailing ones, \(E_1\gg E_L\); PQ requires something closer to a flat profile. A user- chosen hyperparameter \(\kappa\ge 1\) specifies a cap \(\tau=\kappa\bar{E}\) on how much energy a level may carry, where \(\bar{E}=\sum_\ell E_\ell/L\) is the average; \(\kappa=1\) forces perfect equalization; larger \(\kappa\) allows leading levels to remain richer. We sweep levels from front to back, leaving any level with \(E_\ell\le\tau\) unchanged. At a level \(\ell\) that violates the cap, \(E_\ell>\tau\), we apply a Haar-random orthogonal rotation to its dimensions along with a minimal suffix of subsequent dimensions--so that the rotated level’s expected energy drops to \(\tau\). As the rotation is orthogonal, it preserves total energy, redistributing the surplus. This is the _Robin Hood_ metaphor--a rich leading level spills into poorer trailing ones to meet the cap. The composition is orthogonal, preserving soundness, while the per-vector storage and runtime are identical to vanilla PCA. As a side benefit, the intra-level Haar rotation by _U_ makes the residual coordinates isotropic, which the analysis of Section 5 relies on for the \(\epsilon\)-relaxation result of Proposition 5.3. Figure 2 reports the per-level tail energy on each of our six datasets for three transforms: raw (no rotation), PCA-only, and PCA+Shaping (the full shaped transform with the shown hyperparameter \(\kappa\)). PCA-only attains the strongest pruning and determines the compaction coefficient \(\alpha\) used in our cost model (Section 5). PCA+Shaping forfeits some compaction to attain level energies that fit within the cap \(\tau\), for the sake of IVFPQ; the gap between the two curves is small, as Procedure 1 only applies when a level exceeds the cap. The resulting transform is simultaneously amenable to accretive pruning _and_ product quantization--allowing Panorama to work with IVFPQ while maintaining high recall. ## 5 THE COST MODEL Section 4 surfaced a single empirical quantity--the PCA tail-decay rate \(\alpha\)--that characterizes how quickly the residual energy of an embedding collapses under the PCA basis. This section turns \(\alpha\) into a quantitative model of Panorama’s refinement cost. We first justify PCA as the energy-optimal basis (§5.1), then derive the core scaling law \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}]\lesssim Nd/\alpha\) (§5.2), and finally extend the bound to out-of-distribution queries (§5.3) and to the speed--recall knob \(\epsilon\) (§5.4). Each result is paired with a direct empirical comparison; full proofs appear in Appendix A. We use \(f\lesssim g\) to denote upper-bound scaling after the finite-sample constants in the model have been made explicit. ### 5.1 Choice of Basis §4.1 established that PCA is the energy-optimal orthogonal basis: no transform leaves less expected energy \(\sum_{j>m}\lambda_j\) in the trailing coordinates at any level _m_. How fast that tail shrinks is, however, a property of each dataset. Spectral theory provides a strong prior: analytic covariance kernels on a compact domain produce geometrically- decaying Mercer eigenvalues [31], and smooth-activation neural embeddings inherit this through their tangent kernel [9]. Figure 2 confirms it empirically--across all six benchmarks, the PCA tail collapses as \(e^{-\alpha m/d}\), with mean absolute fit error below 0.04. The fitted \(\alpha\) is the single empirical input to everything that follows. ### 5.2 Expected Refinement Cost Panorama prunes a candidate at level _m_ when its level-_m_ lower bound exceeds the running _k_-th best distance _dk_. Equivalently, pruning fires when the gap between the true squared distance and the lower bound drops below the _pruning margin_ \(\Delta(\mathbf{x}):=\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-d_k.\) True _k_-nearest neighbors satisfy \(\Delta\le 0\) by definition and are never pruned. Non-nearest candidates have positive margin in expectation: in high dimensions, query-database distances tightly concentrate around a mean \(\mu\), while _dk_ tracks the lower tail of distances seen so far. A Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz argument [39] on the empirical CDF places _dk_ a slowly-growing number of standard deviations below \(\mu\), so a typical non-nearest candidate has \(\Delta>0\) with high probability. Combining Cauchy-Schwarz with the exponential tail of §5.1 and a bounded-norm condition \(\|T(\mathbf{x})\|\le R\) (giving the prefactor _C_0:=4_R_2), the level-_m_ gap satisfies \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-\mathrm{LB}^m(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\le C_0e^{-\alpha m/d}.\) Pruning fires at the smallest _m_ for which this gap drops below \(\Delta\), giving capped per-candidate depth \(\rho\approx\mathrm{min}\{d,(d/\alpha)[\mathrm{ln}(C_0/\Delta)]_+\}\). Summing \(\rho\) over _N_ candidates and absorbing the averaged margin terms into a finite-sample constant _c_ yields the central result of the section. Proposition 5.1. _Under exponential PCA tail decay, bounded vector norms, and concentrated query-distance distributions, the expected number of coordinate evaluations Panorama performs over N candidates satisfies_ \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}]\lesssim\frac{c\cdot Nd}{\alpha}.\) Here, _c_ is a finite-sample margin constant that absorbs the averaged per-candidate margin terms. _Proof sketch._ The argument has three pieces. First, we turn the energy-decay rate \(\alpha\) into a per-candidate pruning depth bound. Second, we model the pruning margin \(\Delta\) through the order-statistic structure of the running threshold _dk_. Third, we sum the capped per- candidate depths over the _N_ candidates and absorb the averaged margin terms into the finite-sample constant _c_. _(a) Pruning depth._ Combining the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality with the exponential PCA tail and the bounded-norm condition, the gap between the true squared distance and the level-_m_ lower bound is: \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-\mathrm{LB}^m(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\le 4\sqrt{R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(m,d)}R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(m,d)}}\)
\(\approx 4\|\mathbf{q}\|\|\mathbf{x}\|e^{-\alpha m/d}\le C_0e^{-\alpha m/d},\) where the first step is Cauchy-Schwarz, the second applies the exponential tail to query and database, and the third uses the bounded- norm condition along with the definition _C_0:=4_R_2. Pruning occurs when this gap drops below the margin \(\Delta\), i.e., at the smallest _m_ with \(C_0e^{-\alpha m/d}\le\Delta\). Solving for _m_ gives the per-candidate pruning depth \(\rho\approx\mathrm{min}\big\{d,\frac{d}{\alpha}\big[\mathrm{ln}\big(\frac{C_0}{\Delta}\big)\big]_+\big\}.\) This depth is proportional to \(d/\alpha\) and logarithmic in the margin.

_(b) Margin from a Gaussian order statistic._ The threshold _dk_ is, by construction, the _k_-th order statistic among processed squared distances. Intuitively, after processing \(i\gg k\) candidates, _dk_ tracks the lower tail of the distance distribution: if distances cluster around mean \(\mu\), then _dk_ sits a (slowly growing) number of standard deviations _below_ \(\mu\) and stays below \(\mu\). A typical non-nearest candidate has true squared distance close to \(\mu\), so its margin \(\Delta=\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-d_k\) is typically positive. Formally, under the Gaussian distance approximation, the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz (DKW) inequality \[39\] on the empirical distance CDF bounds the threshold by \(d_k\le\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(k/(i+1)+\epsilon_i)\) with high probability, where \(\epsilon_i=\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{ln(1/\delta)/i}\right)\) and \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. For \(k\checkmark i\) and \(k/(i+1)+\epsilon_i<1/2\), the quantile is negative, so the margin satisfies \(\Delta\unknown-\sigma\Phi^{-1}(k/(i+1)+\epsilon_i)>0\) with high probability. The exact union bound is in the technical report. _(c) Aggregation._ Summing the pruning depth \(\rho\) over all _N_ candidates and substituting the margin estimate, we get: \(\mathbb{E}[\text{Cost}]\le c\cdot\frac{Nd}{\alpha},\) where the constant \(c=c(R,\sigma,k,N)\) is the averaged, capped log- margin term from steps (a) and (b). It is bounded and data-dependent. 3 confirms that the measured scanned fraction tracks \(1/\alpha\) within a small constant on our data; empirically the effective constant is order-one and close to 1, so the dominant scaling is \(\mathbb{E}[\text{Cost}]\lesssim Nd/\alpha\). □ _Empirical Validation._ Panorama beats the brute-force cost _Nd_ whenever \(\alpha\) exceeds the effective margin constant, with speedup scaling as \(\alpha/c\). The cost model is checked on two axes. First, Proposition 5.1 predicts that the fraction of dimensions evaluated will scale as \(1/\alpha\). 3 reports the measured fraction alongside the theoretical \(1/\alpha\) on each dataset: the prediction tracks measurement within a small factor across all six benchmarks, so the leading \(1/\alpha\) term governs the speedup. Second, if Panorama evaluates a fraction _p_ of the dimensions, ideal scaling predicts a wall-clock speedup of 1_/p_. Figure 13 plots this semi-empirical prediction against measured QPS. On IVFFlat the points sit on the diagonal; on IVFPQ they exceed it, since the sub-quantizer-major layout of §6.2 unlocks cache benefits beyond what the cost model captures. The algorithmic pruning we predict translates faithfully into measured throughput. ## 5.3 Out-of-Distribution Robustness When a query is drawn from a different distribution than the indexed data--adversarial inputs, cross-domain transfer, modality shifts--its tail energy decays at a rate \(\alpha_q\) distinct from the database rate \(\alpha_x\). The Cauchy-Schwarz remainder depends on the geometric mean \(\sqrt{e^{-\alpha_qm/d}\cdot e^{-\alpha_xm/d}}\), so the effective decay rate becomes the _arithmetic mean_ \(\alpha_\text{eff}=\frac{\alpha_q+\alpha_x}{2}.\) Substituting this effective rate into Proposition 5.1 gives the corresponding robustness bound. Proposition 5.2 (Out-of-distribution cost). _If query and database tail energies decay at rates_ \(\alpha_q\) _and_ \(\alpha_x\)_, respectively, and the OOD candidate stream has margin constant c_ood_, then the expected_ _coordinate-evaluation cost satisfies_ \(\mathbb{E}[\text{Cost}_\text{ood}]\lesssim\frac{2c_\text{ood}Nd}{\alpha_q+\alpha_x}.\) _Proof sketch._ The proof of Proposition 5.1 remains unchanged _except_ for the per-candidate pruning depth bound that uses the tail- decay assumption. We revise that step with separate decay rates. The Cauchy-Schwarz remainder depends on the geometric mean of the two tail energies, \(\sqrt{R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(m,d)}R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(m,d)}}\). With the exponential tail holding separately for query and database, this becomes: \(\sqrt{R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(m,d)}R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(m,d)}}\approx\|\mathbf{q}\|\|\mathbf{x}\|\sqrt{e^{-\alpha_qm/d}e^{-\alpha_xm/d}}\)
\(=\|\mathbf{q}\|\|\mathbf{x}\|e^{-(\alpha_q+\alpha_x)m/(2d)}.\) In effect, the level-_m_ gap decays exponentially with rate \(\alpha_\text{eff}=(\alpha_q+\alpha_x)/2\). Substituting \(\alpha_\text{eff}\) into the depth formula of Proposition 5.1 gives \(\rho_\text{ood}\approx min\big\{d,\frac{2d}{\alpha_q+\alpha_x}\big[ln\left(\frac{C_0}{\Delta}\right)\big]_+\big\}.\) Aggregating across _N_ candidates and absorbing the averaged OOD margin constant _c_ood yields the claimed cost. When the shift changes only tail compaction, _c_ood=_c_; if it also changes the distance distribution, _c_ood reflects the changed margin terms. □ _Interpretation._ As the OOD bound follows the _arithmetic mean_ of the two rates, in the worst case a query halves \(\alpha_\text{eff}\). A fully out-of- distribution query, \(\alpha_q\rightarrow 0\), leaves the leading term at \(2c_\text{ood}Nd/\alpha_x\), with a two-fold slowdown over Proposition 5.1 when the margin constant is unchanged. Panorama robustly benefits from a well-compacted database regardless of the query, as we confirm empirically with Hephaestus OOD workloads (Figure 12): Panorama remains competitive at all relative-contrast levels, while its speedup degrades gracefully as queries harden. Concretely, speedup degrades monotonically from \(25.1\times\) on the easiest workload to \(12.1\times\) on the hardest--a regime where probabilistic baselines either lose recall or cease to scale. ## 5.4 The \(\varepsilon\)-Relaxation Equation (4) defines the relaxed score used by Panorama: it scales the Cauchy-Schwarz correction by a scalar \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\), replacing 2_Cm_ with \(2\varepsilon C^m\), where \(C^m=\sqrt{R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(m,d)}R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(m,d)}}\) is the worst-case residual coupling. Setting \(\varepsilon=1\) corresponds to the adversarial geometry in which Cauchy-Schwarz is tight; in high dimensions, however, this geometry is atypical--the residual coordinates of non-near- neighbors are nearly isotropic on the sphere, and their inner products are far smaller than the worst case. Let \(\rho_m:=\pi_m/C^m\in[-1,1]\) denote the normalized residual inner product, where \(\pi_m=\sum_{j>m}T(\mathbf{q})_jT(\mathbf{x})_j\) is the true residual contribution. The worst case \(\rho_m=-1\) recovers the 4_Cm_ gap underlying Proposition 5.1; under residual isotropy--realized on non-near-neighbor pairs by the intra-block rotation of §4.2--the typical case is \(\rho_m\approx 0\), giving a sharper \(2\varepsilon C^m\) gap. Re-deriving the per-candidate depth with this sharper gap produces an additive shift of \((d/\alpha)ln\varepsilon\).

Proposition 5.3. _Under residual isotropy for non-near-neighbor pairs and_ \(c_\mathrm{typ}+\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon>0\)_, the expected cost under_ \(\varepsilon\)_-relaxation satisfies_ \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}_\varepsilon]\lesssim\frac{Nd\left(c_\mathrm{typ}+\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon\right)}{\alpha}.\) _With observed c_typ≈1_, this simplifies to_ \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}_\varepsilon]\lesssim Nd(1+\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon)/\alpha\) _over the validity range_ \(\varepsilon>1/e\). _Proof sketch._ The argument follows the three-part structure of Proposition 5.1 (per-candidate pruning depth, margin estimate, aggregation), where step (a) uses the typical-case gap. We substitute \(\rho_m\approx 0\) from the residual-isotropy assumption into the gap identity, yielding \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-\mathrm{LB}_\varepsilon^m\approx 2\varepsilon C^m\), and apply the exponential tail to the geometric mean inside _Cm_ followed by the bounded-norm condition: \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-\mathrm{LB}_\varepsilon^m(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\approx 2\varepsilon C^m\approx 2\varepsilon\|\mathbf{q}\|\|\mathbf{x}\|e^{-\alpha m/d}\)
\(\le 2\varepsilon R^2e^{-\alpha m/d},\) where the first ≈ is from the typical-case substitution, the second ≈ applies the exponential tail to both factors of _Cm_, and the final \(\le\) follows from bounded norms. Pruning occurs at the smallest _m_ for which this gap falls below the margin, i.e., \(2\varepsilon R^2e^{-\alpha m/d}\le\Delta\). Solving for _m_ gives the per-candidate pruning depth \(\rho_\varepsilon\approx\frac{d}{\alpha}\mathrm{ln}\left(\frac{2R^2}{\Delta}\right)+\frac{d}{\alpha}\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon.\) The first term is the typical-case pruning depth at \(\varepsilon=1\). It differs from the strict worst-case depth of Proposition 5.1 by carrying 2_Cm_ instead of 4_Cm_, and is absorbed into the empirical typical-case constant. The second term is new: a constant additive shift of \(\frac{d}{\alpha}\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon\) per candidate that relies on the typical-case substitution \(\rho_m\approx 0\). Since \(\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon\le 0\) for \(\varepsilon\le 1\), the shift is negative, shrinking the pruning depth. Summing over _N_ candidates yields \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}_\varepsilon]\lesssim\frac{Nd}{\alpha}\left(c_\mathrm{typ}+\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon\right)\), and the observed _c_typ≈1 gives the proposition. □ _On the formal validity range._ The asymptotic formula requires \(c_\mathrm{typ}+\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon>0\). Setting _c_typ=1 gives the conventional threshold \(\varepsilon>1/e\approx 0.37\); the actual threshold is dataset-dependent. Below this threshold, the pruning depth \(\rho_\varepsilon\) becomes negative, indicating that the bound clears the margin already at level zero, i.e., the relaxation is so aggressive that a candidate may be pruned before any coordinate is read. This is an artifact of the asymptotic; in this regime the speedup is determined by other factors (e.g., the rate at which the heap warms up) and \(\varepsilon\) should be empirically tuned. _Speedup vs. recall._ Proposition 5.3 characterizes the speed side of the tradeoff. Pruning at \(\varepsilon<1\) can discard true _k_-nearest neighbors when \(\rho_m>\varepsilon\) and the resulting overestimate crosses the running threshold. The resulting recall loss depends on the dataset-specific distribution of \(\rho_m\) for true _k_-NN pairs, shown on the right panel of Figure 10. _Additive vs. multiplicative gain._ The \(\varepsilon\)-relaxation is _additive_ on the per-candidate pruning depth, in contrast to the multiplicative \(1/\alpha\) scaling of the base model. Moderate values of \(\varepsilon\) (0.7-0.9) can thus produce a noticeable QPS shift even without large changes to the leading \(1/\alpha\) scaling, while preserving near-perfect recall. _Empirical Validation._ The right panel of Figure 10 sweeps \(\varepsilon\) on Panorama-IVFFlat over Ada and overlays the \(1/(1+\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon)\) prediction against measured QPS. Integrating Panorama into this system required carefully tailoring components to each method. We describe these components here. ### 6.1 IndexIVFFlatPanorama IVFFlat [24] partitions the dataset into _n_list clusters via _k_-means and scans the nearest _n_probe clusters to a query. Faiss stores each cluster’s points row-major (cluster[point][dim]). This storage scheme is suboptimal because under an effective pruning threshold, Panorama evaluates only the leading dimensions of each candidate, which with a row-major layout causes inefficient large strides in memory accesses. _Level-major batched layout._ Thus, we organize each cluster into batches of _B_ vectors in level-major order, generalizing the layout of PDX [28]: within a batch, all _B_ vectors’ level-\(\ell\) slices are stored contiguously, followed by all _B_ level-\(\ell+1\) slices, and so on. Figure 3 shows a simple example where _L_=30 levels and _B_=4 candidates. By this layout, distance computation within a single level proceeds over all _B_ points with a sequential stride. Pruning decisions are made by the pruning threshold set in the previous batch. In effect, overly large values of _B_ will lead to pruning decisions based on a stale pruning threshold, while overly small values of _B_ will introduce additional branches. Increasing _B_ from 1 to 1024 causes the increase in performance between **A1** and **A2** in Figure 9. _Per-level workflow._ Within each batch, at each level \(\ell\), Panorama executes three phases over the active candidate set stored as an array of _active indices_: (1) _Compute_ partial dot products of the query slice corresponding to level \(\ell\) for each active candidate; (2) _Update_ each candidate’s running distance and test its Cauchy–Schwarz lower bound against the current _k_th nearest neighbor; (3) _Consolidate_ the surviving active indices for the next level. A naive implementation would fuse all three phases into a single branchy loop. We instead implement them as three independently vectorizable kernels. ## 6.2 IndexIVFPQPanorama

IVFPQ [25] splits each vector into _M_ subvectors and quantizes each against a 2_<sup>n</sup>_bits-entry codebook, replacing the per-candidate float dot product with a sum of _M_ look-up-table (LUT) lookups over 1- byte codes. We preserve the three-phase workflow of Section 6.1, but revamp Phases 1 and 3 for PQ codes.

_Sub-quantizer-major layout._ A direct import of the IVFFlat level- major layout would store _M/L_ contiguous bytes per candidate per level. Since _M/L_ bytes is typically much smaller than modern SIMD vector widths, wide register loads would suffer from lane underutilization. We thus transpose the data _within_ a level, storing the _m_- th sub-quantizer’s code contiguously across a batch of _B_ candidates. A single 64-byte SIMD load thus fetches the same sub-quantizer’s code for 64 candidates in parallel. Figure 4 shows a toy example with _M=_480 subvectors, _L=_16 levels, _B=_4 candidates.

This transposition also benefits temporal locality. In standard IVFPQ, evaluating a single vector requires reading from every sub- quantizer’s slice of the LUT. As the full LUT can easily exceed 128 KB, this vector-by-vector access pattern heavily thrashes the L1 cache. By processing the same sub-quantizer across 64 candidates simultaneously, our layout keeps a tiny 256-entry LUT slice pinned in the L1 cache for the entire batch, reducing cache thrashing. In effect, even if we disable Panorama’s pruning, the transposed layout alone outperforms Faiss’s heavily-optimized IVFPQ baseline<tbc>

<tbc>by up to 2\(\times\) (Figure 13). This approach applies the transposed data layouts of BitWeaving and ByteSlice [15, 30] to PQ.

_IVFPQ: Compute_ collects per-level distances for each batch at level \(\ell\) by a single process\_level kernel. We use i32gather to index one sub-quantizer’s LUT slice for 16 candidates in parallel; combined with the sub-quantizer-major layout, it unlocks SIMD- rate distance updates over packed PQ codes.

_IVFPQ: Update_ reuses the IVFFlat survivor-mask kernel verbatim; PQ codes never enter the prune loop.

_IVFPQ: Consolidate_ packs survivors’ codes into a dense buffer 64 candidates at a time, avoiding both the SIMD lane underutilization of processing pruned slots and the scattered byte reads that would break the contiguous layout. Two fast paths bracket this step: when no candidate is pruned we alias the original code pointer and skip consolidation entirely, and once fewer than _B/_<sup>16</sup> candidates remain we drop vectorization and traverse the active-index array directly in the compute phase.

## 6.3 IndexHNSWFlatPanorama

HNSW [37] traverses its graph greedily, iteratively popping the closest frontier vertex from a candidate heap to compute its neighbors’ exact distances. Neighbors closer than the _k_<sup>th</sup> best distance enter a global result heap and the candidate heap. Filtering and refinement are thus interleaved, yielding scattered, memory-bound accesses governed by the graph topology.

Because Panorama’s level-wise evaluation exacerbates HNSW’s memory-bound, scattered accesses, we introduce three structural adaptations to hide cache latencies and preserve traversal stability. First, _K-pop block evaluation_: we relax strict greedy routing by popping multiple vertices simultaneously from the candidate heap, processing their combined unvisited neighbors in dense SIMD blocks of 64. Second, _coefficient inlining_: we embed the precomputed residual energies directly into a small prefix header of each database vector, reducing cache misses by one per candidate. Third, _partial distance routing_: candidates pruned at level \(\ell\) are not discarded, but pushed back into the candidate heap keyed by a partial distance estimate--calculated as the midpoint of the lower and upper bounds ((LB + UB)/2). This estimate acts as a proxy to seed further exploration without requiring full distance evaluations.

## 6.4 IndexRefinePanorama

An increasingly popular ANNS pipeline uses PQ for a fast first pass (Faiss FastScan [12, 45]) and then _refines_ the top-\(k'\) candidates with exact distances on a flat float index. Panorama also plugs into this refine step: IndexRefinePanorama forwards the base index’s top-\(k'\) labels to an inner IndexFlatPanorama that stores vectors in row-major order and runs Panorama with _B_=1--refinement targets a scattered ID list, so the level-major batched layout of Section 6.1 is inapplicable. As with HNSW, we process candidates in groups of 64: a one-pass sweep over the block’s IDs absorbs random-access latency; then the per-level dot-product kernel runs across the block with the query slice pinned in registers.

### 6.5 Memory footprint

Panorama precomputes per-point cumulative tail energies for the Cauchy-Schwarz bound: 4(_L_+1) bytes per point, O(_nL_) in total. The overhead per index family relative to the base storage is:

\(\bullet\) **IVFFlat** / **Refine**: \(\frac{L+1}{d}\) , dwarfed by the 4_d_-byte vector.<tbc>

\(\bullet\) **HNSW**: \(\frac{L+1}{d+2M_\mathrm{HNSW}}\) , where the \(2M_\mathrm{HNSW}\times 4\) bytes denominator term represents the memory overhead of each node’s graph topology (the adjacency lists). Because the graph structure itself consumes substantial memory, the relative Panorama overhead is further diluted compared to purely flat structures.<tbc>

\(\bullet\) **IVFPQ**: \(\frac{4(L+1)}{M_\mathrm{PQ}}\) , the only nontrivial case, since PQ codes are al ready 1B per dimension. While standard 8-bit scalar quantization could compress these values and cut the overhead by 4x, evaluating the impact of this quantization noise on the exactness of our accretive pruning bounds is left to future work.

## 7 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

We evaluate Panorama across three axes: (i) end-to-end QPS under fully-recall-preserving exhaustive search, (ii) QPS vs. recall when integrated into state-of-the-art indexes, and (iii) the isolated performance impacts of our algorithmic knobs and systems optimizations. Across these evaluations, Panorama consistently delivers tremendous performance, yielding up to a 28.9\(\times\) speedup over Faiss’ baselines while preserving the recall of the underlying index.

_Methodology._ We run three repetitions of 1000 10-NN queries randomly sampled from each benchmark’s query set and report averages. We evaluate all methods using a single thread on an Intel Xeon Gold 5416S CPU @ 2.0 GHz with 128 GB DDR5-6400 RAM, running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. Binaries are compiled with GCC 13.3.0 using -03 and AVX-512 optimization. We wrap each Panorama index with Faiss’ IndexPreTransform to apply the PCA transformation and include its overhead in the reported query time. We also minimally modify the PDX source code to support batched queries, batched transformations, and feature-processing metrics.

## 7.4 Transform contribution

Figure 8 isolates the contribution of the orthogonal transform. On contiguous indexes, raw-vector Panorama already accelerates search via systems-optimized pruning, but the PCA-shaped basis consistently amplifies these gains by tightening the Cauchy– Schwarz bound (Proposition 5.1). On GIST (\(R\ge 0.95\)), PCA alone scales Panorama’s QPS by 12.3× on IVFFlat and 7.3× on IVFPQ over the raw baseline. Conversely, on non-contiguous structures like HNSW and FastScan-Refine, Panorama depends entirely on the transform: raw Panorama-HNSW drops to 0.80×, whereas adding PCA yields a 2.83× speedup. Because pointer-based graph traversals suffer a cache miss on nearly every candidate look-up, runtime is heavily dominated by memory latency rather than distance arithmetic. By Amdahl’s Law [2], optimizing compute under such memory-bound conditions yields negligible returns, meaning raw pruning’s minor arithmetic savings cannot offset its overhead.

However, each extra level introduces branch-prediction overhead and disrupts CPU prefetching by breaking predictable memory strides. **_Batch Size (B)_**. Throughput peaks at _B_=1024 (6.6\(\times\) over un- batched), our standard across all datasets. Larger _B_ degrades throughput through threshold staleness: all _B_ points are pruned against the previous batch’s bound, so oversized batches scan an inflated fraction of dimensions before the threshold updates, decaying to 3.8\(\times\) at _B_=8192.

## 8 CONCLUSION

We introduced Panorama, an accretive refinement layer that integrates broadly into modern vector indexes. Panorama accumulates _L_<sub>2</sub> contributions along the PCA basis and prunes candidates the moment a tight Cauchy-Schwarz lower bound exceeds the running _k_-NN threshold; we prove its expected cost scales as \(\mathcal{O}(Nd/\alpha)\) in the dataset’s spectral decay rate \(\alpha\). Across six datasets and four index families (IVFPQ/Flat, HNSW, and PQ-refine), Panorama outperforms the baselines at any target recall, delivering up to 28.9\(\times\) speedups, while remaining robust on OOD queries. It has been upstreamed into Faiss and ships in its official releases.

This appendix gives full derivations for Propositions 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3, plus the PCA energy-optimality result. Numbering matches the main paper; auxiliary results use a separate “A.” sequence.

### A.1 Notation and assumptions

We adopt the notation of the main paper. All vectors lie in R_<sup>d</sup>_. For an orthogonal transform _T_ and a level \(0\le m\le d\), the _tail energy_ of a vector **v** is<tbc>

\(R_{T(\mathbf{v})}^{(m,d)}:=\sum_{j=m+1}^dT(\mathbf{v})_j^2.\)

<tbc>The level-_m_ Cauchy–Schwarz lower bound on \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2\) is

\(\mathrm{LB}^m(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})=R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(0,d)}+R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(0,d)}-2\left(p^{(0,m)}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})+\sqrt{R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(m,d)}R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(m,d)}}\right),\) (5)

<tbc>where \(p^{(0,m)}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})=\sum_{j=1}^MT(\mathbf{q})_jT(\mathbf{x})_j\). The \(\varepsilon\)-relaxed bound re places the second factor by \(2\varepsilon\sqrt{R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(m,d)}R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(m,d)}}\), with \(\varepsilon=1\) recov ering (5).

Panorama maintains a running threshold \(\tau\), the squared distance of the _k_th nearest neighbour found so far (written _d<sub>k</sub>_ in the main paper). A candidate **x** is pruned at level _m_ if \(\mathrm{LB}^m(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})>\tau\), equivalently if the gap

\(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-\mathrm{LB}^m(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\le\Delta:=\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-\tau.\)

We call \(\Delta\) the _pruning margin_. In strict mode (\(\varepsilon=1\)), true _k_-nearest neighbours satisfy \(\Delta\le 0\) and are never pruned by a valid lower bound; the analysis below shows that for non-near-neighbours \(\Delta\) is positive with high probability and the gap shrinks fast enough to prune at \(m\checkmark d\).

_Asymptotic notation._ We use \(f(n)\lesssim g(n)\) for model upper-bound scaling after constants are explicit, and _f(n_)∼_cg(n_) for asymptotic equivalence with constant _c\>_0.

_Assumptions._ The proofs rest on the following assumptions, reproduced here for self-containment.

**Assumption A1** (Exponential PCA tail energy)**.** We take _T_ to be the PCA basis of the dataset. On real embeddings its tail energy decays exponentially,

\(R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(m,d)}\approx\|\mathbf{x}\|^2e^{-\alpha m/d},\)

where \(\alpha>0\) is the per-dataset decay rate read directly off the PCA spectrum. This exponential profile is an empirical property of the PCA basis, which we verify directly: the mean absolute fit error of the model is below 0.04 on every dataset (main paper, energy-compaction figure). The ≈ records exactly this finite-sample modelling claim.

**Assumption A2** (Bounded norms)**.** There is a constant _R_ such that \(\|T(\mathbf{x})\|\le R\) for every **x** in the dataset and every query **q**. We write _C_<sub>0</sub>:=4_R_<sup>2</sup>.

**Assumption A3** (Gaussian distance model)**.** For a fixed query **q**, the squared distances \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2\) in the candidate stream are modelled as i.i.d. draws from a Gaussian with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). The exact distribution is chi-square-like and the candidate stream produced by an ANN index is not literally i.i.d.; the Gaussian order- statistic calculation is the tractable cost model whose constants are checked empirically.

**Assumption A4** (One dimension per level)**.** The proof reasons at the finest pruning granularity, _L=d_, \(m_\ell=\ell\).

A fifth assumption (residual isotropy, A5) is introduced and used only in Section A.5.

## A.2 PCA minimises expected tail energy

**Lemma A.1** (Ky Fan)**.** _Let_ \(\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) _be symmetric positive semidefinite with eigenvalues_ \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge 0\)_. For every_ \(m\in\{1,\dots,d\}\),

\(\mathrm{max}_{T\in\mathrm{O}(d)}\sum_{j=1}^m(T\Sigma T^\top)_{jj}=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j,\)

_with the maximum attained when the first m rows of T span the eigenspace associated with the top-m eigenvalues of_ \(\Sigma\).

Proof (sketch). The diagonal of \(T\Sigma T^\top\) is majorised by the eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\) (Schur–Horn theorem). For any _m_, the partial sum of the _m_ largest diagonal entries is at most the partial sum of the _m_ largest eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\). Equality is attained by the orthogonal transform whose first _m_ rows span the corresponding eigenspace. See Horn and Johnson \[21\], Section 4.3 for the full proof. \(\square\)

**Proposition** (PCA energy-optimality; cf. main paper Sections 4.1 and 5.1)**.** _Let_ \(X\in\mathbb{R}^d\) _be a centred random vector_ (E\[_X_\]=**0**_) with covariance_ \(\Sigma=\mathbb{E}[XX^\top]\) _having eigenvalues_ \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge 0\)_. For any orthogonal_ \(T\in\mathrm{O}(d)\) _and any_ \(m\in\{1,\dots,d-1\}\),

\(\mathbb{E}\big[R_{T(X)}^{(m,d)}\big]\ge\sum_{j=m+1}^d\lambda_j,\)

_with equality when the rows of T are eigenvectors of_ \(\Sigma\) _ordered by decreasing eigenvalue._

Proof. For any orthogonal _T_,

\(\mathbb{E}\big[(TX)_j^2\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[(TX)(TX)^\top\big]_{jj}=\big(T\mathbb{E}[XX^\top]T^\top\big)_{jj}=(T\Sigma T^\top)_{jj}.\)

Summing over _j\>m_,

\(\mathbb{E}\big[R_{T(X)}^{(m,d)}\big]=\sum_{j=m+1}^d(T\Sigma T^\top)_{jj}.\)

Orthogonal conjugation preserves the trace, so

\(\sum_{j=1}^d(T\Sigma T^\top)_{jj}=\mathrm{Tr}(T\Sigma T^\top)=\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j.\)

Therefore

\(\mathbb{E}\big[R_{T(X)}^{(m,d)}\big]=\sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j-\sum_{j=1}^m(T\Sigma T^\top)_{jj}.\)

By Lemma A.1,

\(\sum_{j=1}^m(T\Sigma T^\top)_{jj}\le\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j,\)

with equality when the first _m_ rows of _T_ span the top-_m_ eigenspace of \(\Sigma\). Substituting,

\(\mathbb{E}\big[R_{T(X)}^{(m,d)}\big]\ge\sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j=\sum_{j=m+1}^d\lambda_j,\)

with equality precisely when _T_ is the PCA basis. \(\square\)

## A.3 Proposition 5.1: Expected refinement cost

This section derives the expected refinement cost of Panorama under the Gaussian candidate-stream model. The argument has three ingredients: a high-probability model for the running _k_th threshold, a Cauchy–Schwarz pruning-depth bound, and an averaged finite-sample margin constant.

Panorama maintains a pruning threshold \(\tau\), the squared distance of the _k_th nearest neighbour found so far. For analytical tractability we model \(\tau_i\) as the _k_th order statistic among _i_ i.i.d. draws from the distance distribution, acknowledging that the algorithm’s threshold actually arises from a mixture of exact and pruned candidates.

**Lemma A.2** (High-probability bound on the sampled threshold via DKW)**.** _Let the squared distances be i.i.d. with CDF F. For any_ \(\epsilon\in(0,1)\)_, with probability at least_ \(1-2e^{-2i\epsilon^2}\) _(Dvoretzky-Kiefer- Wolfowitz [39]), the k_th _order statistic_ \(\tau_i\) _satisfies_

\(F^{-1}\big(max\big\{0,\frac{k}{i+1}-\epsilon\big\}\big)\le\tau_i\le F^{-1}\big(min\big\{1,\frac{k}{i+1}+\epsilon\big\}\big).\)

_Under the Gaussian assumption A3 (_\(F(r)=\Phi((r-\mu)/\sigma)\)_), this gives in particular_

\(\tau_i\le\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}\big(\frac{k}{i+1}+\epsilon\big)\text{\textit{with probability at least}}1-2e^{-2i\epsilon^2}.\)

Proof. Let _F<sub>i</sub>_ be the empirical CDF of the first _i_ distances. The DKW inequality gives \(Pr(sup_t|F_i(t)-F(t)|>\epsilon)\le 2e^{-2i\epsilon^2}\). On the event sup_<sub>t</sub>_ \(|F_i-F|\le\epsilon\) we have \(F(t)-\epsilon\le F_i(t)\le F(t)+\epsilon\) for all _t_; monotonicity of _F_<sup>-1</sup> then gives \(F^{-1}(u-\epsilon)\le F_i^{-1}(u)\le F^{-1}(u+\epsilon)\) for all \(u\in(0,1)\). Taking _u=k/(i_+1) and recalling \(\tau_i=F_i^{-1}(k/(i+1))\) yields the two-sided bound. Under A3, \(F^{-1}(p)=\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p)\), which gives the Gaussian form. \(\square\)

A new candidate is tested against \(\tau_i\); in the Gaussian model, a representative non-near-neighbour candidate has squared distance near the mean \(\mu\). This lets us define a model margin.

**Definition A.3** (Model margin \(\Delta_i\))**.** Fix \(\epsilon_i\in(0,1)\) and set the sampled _k_th-NN threshold upper bound

\(K_i:=\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}\big(\frac{k}{i+1}+\epsilon_i\big),\Delta_i:=\mu-K_i=-\sigma\Phi^{-1}\big(\frac{k}{i+1}+\epsilon_i\big).\)

On the DKW event of Lemma A.2, the model threshold is at most _K<sub>i</sub>_. Thus a representative non-near-neighbour candidate at squared distance \(\mu\) has model margin at least \(\Delta_i\). We use \(\Delta_i\) as the per-step representative margin in the cost model; candidate-level fluctuations are absorbed into the averaged constant _C<sub>N</sub>_ below. The margin is positive whenever \(\frac{k}{i+1}+\epsilon_i<\frac{1}{2}\) (so \(\Phi^{-1}(\cdot)<0\)).

_Uniform high-probability schedule._ Fix a target failure probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\) and set<tbc>

\(\epsilon_i:=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2i}ln\frac{2N}{\delta}}.\)

<tbc>By a union bound over \(i\in\{k+1,\dots,N\}\), the event

\(\mathcal{E}_\delta:=\cap_{i=k+1}^N\big\{\tau_i\le\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}\big(\frac{k}{i+1}+\epsilon_i\big)\big\}\)

holds with probability at least \(1-\delta\). All bounds below are stated on \(\mathcal{E}_\delta\).

A candidate **x**_<sub>j</sub>_ is pruned at level _m_ once its lower bound exceeds the threshold. A sufficient condition is that the worst-case lower- bound error falls below the margin of the candidate processed at step _i_:<tbc>

<tbc>By Cauchy-Schwarz the left-hand side is at most four times the geometric mean of the tail energies; applying Assumptions A1 and A2,<tbc>

Performance degrades gracefully rather than collapsing, as long as the database vectors are well-compacted. ## A.5 Proposition 5.3: The \(\varepsilon\)-relaxation Setting \(\varepsilon=1\) uses the exact Cauchy-Schwarz correction 2_Cm_ and preserves recall. That worst-case correction is attained only at the adversarial residual alignment \(\rho_m=-1\); on real, isotropised residuals the typical alignment is \(\rho_m\approx 0\), where the correction is already a factor of two smaller. The \(\varepsilon\)-relaxation exploits this gap: it discounts the correction by a factor \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\), pruning earlier at a controlled, quantifiable cost in recall. We first record the exact gap identity, then state the isotropy assumption that makes the typical case precise, and finally turn it into a cost bound that mirrors Proposition 5.1. The \(\varepsilon\)-relaxed bound is \(\mathrm{LB}_\varepsilon^m(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})=A^m-2\varepsilon C^m,C^m:=\sqrt{R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(m,d)}}R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(m,d)},\) where \(A^m=R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(0,d)}+R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(0,d)}-2p^{(0,m)}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\). Define the residual inner product \(\pi_m=\sum_{j>m}T(\mathbf{q})_jT(\mathbf{x})_j\) and its normalised value \(\rho_m:=\frac{\pi_m}{C^m}\in[-1,1],\) where the bounds follow from Cauchy-Schwarz applied to the residual.

**Lemma A.7** (Gap identity)**.** _For every level m,_ \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-\mathrm{LB}_\varepsilon^m(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})=2C^m(\varepsilon-\rho_m).\) Proof. Direct expansion: \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2=R_{T(\mathbf{q})}^{(0,d)}+R_{T(\mathbf{x})}^{(0,d)}-2\sum_{j=1}^dT(\mathbf{q})_jT(\mathbf{x})_j\)
\(=A^m-2\pi_m.\) Subtracting the relaxed bound, \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2-\mathrm{LB}_\varepsilon^m(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})=(A^m-2\pi_m)-(A^m-2\varepsilon C^m)\)
\(=2(\varepsilon C^m-\pi_m)\)
\(=2C^m(\varepsilon-\rho_m).\square\) At \(\varepsilon=1\) and worst case \(\rho_m=-1\) the gap is 4_Cm_, matching the strict cost bound; at \(\varepsilon=1\) and typical \(\rho_m\approx 0\) the gap is 2_Cm_, a factor of 2 tighter. **Assumption A5** (Residual isotropy)**.** For non-near-neighbour pairs (**q**,**x**), the residual coordinates (_T_(**q**)_j,T_(**x**)_j)j\>m_ are independent and uniformly distributed on the sphere in R_d-m_ (independently for **q** and **x**). Consequently, by standard high-dimensional concentration, \(\rho_m\sim\mathcal{N}\big(0,\frac{1}{d-m}\big)\text{approximately}.\) _Remark._ Assumption A5 is realised by the intra-level isotropization step in the main paper’s variance-shaping transform. It applies only to non-near-neighbour pairs; for true _k_-NN pairs the residuals are correlated (the nearness manifests in the residual), so \(\rho_m\) for true neighbours concentrates strictly above 0. The recall loss at \(\varepsilon<1\) arises precisely from neighbour pairs with \(\rho_m>\varepsilon\). **Lemma A.8** (Pruning depth, \(\varepsilon\)-relaxed)**.** _Under Assumptions A1-A5, for non-near-neighbour candidates and a margin_ \(\Delta>0\)_, the pruning depth at the_ \(\varepsilon\)_-relaxed bound is_ \(d^{(\varepsilon)}(\Delta)\approx\frac{d}{\alpha}\mathrm{ln}\frac{2R^2}{\Delta}+\frac{d}{\alpha}\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon.\) Proof. Under A5, \(\rho_m\) concentrates at 0 with deviation \(1/\sqrt{d-m}\). For_ \(\varepsilon<1\)_, each candidate is pruned_ \((d/\alpha)\mathrm{ln}(1/\varepsilon)\) _dimensions earlier on average than at_ \(\varepsilon=1\) _until the cap at zero dimensions becomes active._ Proof. The argument mirrors the cost proof, with the pruning depth of Lemma A.4 replaced by Lemma A.8. We work on the same high-probability event \(\mathcal{E}_\delta\) (Lemma A.2); the threshold and margin analysis are unchanged. Substituting the margin asymptotic (7) into Lemma A.8 and aggregating as in Proposition 5.1, the additive \((d/\alpha)\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon\) term carries through the sum to give \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}_\varepsilon]\lesssim\frac{Nd}{\alpha}\left(c_\mathrm{typ}+\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon\right),\) where \(c_\mathrm{typ}=\mathrm{ln}(2R^2/\sigma)-\zeta_N\) is the typical-residual counterpart of _CN_, shifted only by ln2 (the typical-case prefactor is 2_R_2 rather than _C_0=4_R_2) and inheriting the same log-log behaviour. Since _c_typ is observed to be ≈1, \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Cost}_\varepsilon]\lesssim\frac{Nd\left(1+\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon\right)}{\alpha}.\square\) _Remark_ (Validity range). The asymptotic requires \(c_\mathrm{typ}+\mathrm{ln}\varepsilon>0\). Setting _c_typ=1 gives the conventional threshold \(\varepsilon>1/e\approx 0.37\); the actual threshold is dataset-dependent. Below it, the formula predicts a negative pruning depth--an artifact: the bound clears the margin already at _m_=0, and the cost is governed by other factors (heap warm-up, fixed per-candidate overhead). In this regime \(\varepsilon\) should be tuned empirically. _Remark_ (Additive vs. multiplicative). The \(\varepsilon\)-relaxation contributes _additively_ to the per-candidate pruning depth, in contrast to the multiplicative \(1/\alpha\) scaling of the base model. A moderate \(\varepsilon=0.7\) shifts the prefactor by ln0.7≈-0.36, enough to produce a noticeable QPS gain without changing the leading \(1/\alpha\) behaviour, while preserving near-perfect recall. Proposition 5.3 characterises the speed side of the \(\varepsilon\) knob. Pruning at \(\varepsilon<1\) discards true _k_-nearest-neighbour pairs whose residual ratio \(\rho_m\) exceeds \(\varepsilon\). The recall loss thus depends on the dataset- specific distribution of \(\rho_m\) for true _k_-NN pairs, which is measurable per dataset (see the \(\varepsilon\) ablation in the main paper). We do not attempt a closed-form recall bound; the \(\rho_m\) distribution for _k_-NN pairs concentrates strictly above 0 (these pairs are correlated, breaking the isotropy of A5), and recall begins to degrade once \(\varepsilon\) falls below the bulk of this distribution.
